result: The patch-walking approach, which involves cleaning and reusing one pipette while maintaining the other, theoretically enables probing almost twice the number of connections compared to traditional methods. Mathematical modeling suggests 80-92% more probed connections for experiments with 10-100 cells using 2-8 pipettes.
evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the theoretical efficiency improvements of patch-walking. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'show convincing results' and that the approach 'can theoretically yield almost twice the number of connections.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the conceptual approach of recording multiple partner cells from another in a step wise manner indeed increases the number of tested connections.' The editor confirms the authors 'present solid evidence that this strategy...has the potential to substantially improve the efficiency.'

result: The automated dual-pipette patch-walking system achieved 71 successful whole cell recordings out of 136 attempts (52.2% success rate) across 136 cells from 7 animals over 7 days. This success rate is comparable to previously reported automated and manual patch clamp systems (43-51% for automated, 30-80% for manual), and coordinating pipette motion via patch-walking does not deteriorate success rates.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the reported success rates without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'show convincing results from recordings in mouse in vitro cortical slices demonstrating the efficient recording of dozens of paired neurons.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'data to show that this approach is able to successfully record from 52% of attempted cells.' The comparisons to prior work are not questioned by any reviewer.

result: From 29 paired recordings (58 bidirectional probed connections) with an average intersomatic distance of 91.6 μm, three synaptic connections were found. This is lower than the 16.9% connection probability predicted by Perin et al. 2011 for this distance, which the authors attribute to biological variation.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises significant concerns about the low connectivity rate (5%), stating 'the robotic system appears primarily suited to probing connections between neurons with greater spatial separation (~100µm ISD)' and suggests 'this limitation could help explain the low connectivity rate.' The reviewer notes the system 'may not reliably detect connections between neurons in close proximity, a potential drawback given that the connectivity is much higher between spatially close neurons.' While the authors attribute the low rate to biological variation, this explanation is not explicitly endorsed by reviewers.

result: The patch-walking system achieved paired recordings in an average of 12.6±7.5 minutes, with cells held in whole cell configuration up to 45 minutes. Of 71 whole cell recordings, 44 paired recordings were achieved, representing 9 more paired recordings than would have been achieved with the traditional method (35 pairs).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'a comparison of measurements shown in Figure 2 to other methods has not been addressed adequately,' indicating that the efficiency claims lack sufficient comparative context. While the raw data on timing and paired recordings is not disputed, the interpretation of these results as demonstrating superior efficiency compared to other methods remains inadequately supported according to this reviewer.

result: A dual-pipette automated patch-walking apparatus was constructed featuring two PatchStar micromanipulators, automated pressure control, custom printed circuit boards for independent pipette control, machine vision-based calibration, and standard electrophysiology equipment including a Multiclamp 700B amplifier and data acquisition boards.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the technical implementation without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes 'the implementation of automated robotic whole-cell patch-clamp techniques from multiple cells simultaneously is a useful addition' and 'the approach using 2 electrodes, which are washed between cells is economically favourable.' The technical details are not questioned by any reviewer.

result: Recordings were performed in mouse somatosensory and primary visual cortex (primarily L2/3, L4, L5) using male C57BL/6 mice (P19-P36). Brain slices (300 μm coronal sections) were prepared using standard protocols with sucrose solution and neuronal aCSF, and recordings were performed at room temperature with constant perfusion.
evaluation: The experimental methods are accepted by reviewers without objection. Reviewer 2 notes that 'morphological identification of neurons is understandably outside the remit of this project - but should be discussed,' indicating acceptance of the basic methodology while requesting additional discussion of cell type identification. No reviewer challenges the slice preparation or recording protocols.

result: The patch-walking algorithm involves user selection of 8-10 healthy cells spread across ~200 μm × 200 μm, with the robot computing distances and assigning the closest cell to each pipette. When one pipette achieves whole cell configuration, it is held while the other attempts new patches. Failed attempts result in pipette cleaning and reassignment to the next closest cell.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the algorithmic approach. Reviewer 1 notes the method involves 'coordinated pipette route-planning and automated pipette cleaning procedures' and that the authors 'show experimental results for a fully automated electrophysiology dual patch-clamp recording approach.' The algorithm description is not challenged by any reviewer.

result: Quality control criteria included access resistance below 40 MΩ (with recording stopped if it exceeded 50 MΩ) and exclusion of cells with decreased seal quality. Connectivity testing followed protocols similar to Perin et al. 2011 and the Allen Institute, with bidirectional testing using current clamp stimulation (5 action potentials at 20 Hz) and voltage clamp recording at -70 mV.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern: 'The revised manuscript does not clearly state which cells were included in the analysis as far as I can see - and indeed cells with Access Resistance >40 MOhm appear to still be included in the data.' This suggests the quality control criteria may not have been consistently applied or clearly reported, creating uncertainty about which recordings were actually included in the final analysis.

result: Patch-walking is recommended for researchers searching for local synaptic connections using small numbers of pipettes. The method offers advantages including reduced tissue damage (one vs. two new pipettes per connection), time savings, more recordings before cell death, and improved accessibility for laboratories without complex multi-pipette setups. The approach can be implemented in both automated and manual recording systems.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'a discussion of the implementation of this approach to manual methods is still lacking,' indicating that claims about manual applicability are inadequately supported. Reviewer 3 expresses broader concerns about applicability: 'While the approach might be valuable in specific research contexts, its overall applicability seems limited' and notes 'Loss of Morphological Information: Unlike traditional multi-patch recording, this approach likely loses all detailed morphology of each recorded neuron.' These concerns suggest the claimed advantages and broad applicability are not fully established.

result: Future applications and extensions of patch-walking are proposed, including: scaling beyond two pipettes with careful collision avoidance, optimal route-planning algorithms (e.g., Monte Carlo Tree), channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping, fluorescent-targeted cell recording, deep cell patching with secondary pipette searching, morphological identification studies, and machine learning for cell type detection and route planning.
evaluation: Reviewers positively acknowledge the discussion of extensions. Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors suggest extensions of their technique while keeping the number of recording pipettes employed and recording rig complexity low, which are important practical technical considerations.' However, Reviewer 3 cautions that 'Scalability Challenges: Scaling this method beyond a two-pipette setup may be difficult. Additional pipettes would introduce significant technical and logistical complexities.' The future directions are accepted as reasonable proposals but with acknowledged limitations.

result: During patch-walking experiments, cell health can decrease over time (as observed in Cell 7), likely due to experiment duration and tissue deformation from pipette movements. A representative synaptic connection was found between cells 1 and 2, with pre-synaptic stimulation eliciting post-synaptic currents.
evaluation: These observational findings are accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes the authors demonstrate 'detection of synaptic connections' and Reviewer 2 confirms the system 'was able to detect 3 pairs in 71 screened neurons.' The technical challenges of tissue deformation are implicitly acknowledged through Reviewer 3's concerns about spatial restrictions and the need for greater separation between neurons.
